ut_green_meadow_crags.blurb: A small, recently developed set of cliffs high in the Uinta Mountains of northeast Utah, around 10,400 feet. The rock is the steep, horizontally cracked quartzite typical of the range, and the lines are traditional: the cracks take cams and nuts, with only a few bolted anchors on top. About twenty routes are known, most of them moderate, roughly 5.6 to 5.8, with a couple of 5.10 lines and a handful of easy ones. The cliffs sit above open meadows, so expect plenty of sun, a relaxed adventure feel and little company. Being at altitude, it is a cooler alternative to the valley heat.

ut_turtle_wall.blurb: A bolted sandstone crag in the desert above Snow Canyon, just outside St. George, past the better-known Chuckawalla Wall. About twenty sport routes run from 5.8 up to the low 5.13s, but the bulk of them fall between 5.11 and 5.12, so it suits climbers who already lead in that range. The stone is steep in places with big pockets, and a natural cave-like arch holds some of the most overhanging lines. The rock is a little soft and sandy rather than loose. The wall faces east, so it catches the morning light and falls into shade as the day goes on, and it has a more wild, outdoorsy feel than the roadside walls.

ut_disappointment_cliffs.blurb: The longest continuous cliff line in the Indian Creek canyon system of southeast Utah, tucked between the Broken Tooth and the Second Meat Wall. Because the sandstone is fractured in places, it holds fewer lines than neighbouring walls, but the ones that exist are all traditional crack climbs. Roughly twenty routes span about 5.9 to 5.13, with most in the 5.10 and 5.11 range and a short list of hard test pieces above. Pullouts along the paved highway serve the middle of the cliff, while dirt roads at either end reach the flanks. Bring a full crack rack, and plan for no more than basic facilities nearby.

ut_boy_scout_cave.blurb: A bouldering spot inside Pioneer Park, on the north edge of St. George in the red desert sandstone. Around twenty problems are packed near a small cave, and the grades are friendly: plenty of V1 to V4 with a few V5s and one V6 at the top end, so it works for beginners and mid-level boulderers alike. It is a short walk north from the paved lot beside the pavilion. This is a busy local park, often full of families, so expect an audience and bring a pad and some patience. Watch for thorny plants near the base of the cave.

ut_sacred_cow_wall.blurb: A crack-climbing wall in Indian Creek, in the sandstone country of southeast Utah, reached from the Meat Wall dirt road off the highway with a walk of roughly 15 to 25 minutes. It holds about twenty traditional lines, with a few toprope and sport options mixed in. The focus is on sustained 5.11 cracks lying very close together, with some 5.10 and several 5.12s and a single 5.13 above. The pitches are long, even by Creek standards, and some are among the best in the canyon. It has grown busier in recent years, so a weekday visit helps. Bring multiples of the usual crack sizes.

ut_distant_drum.blurb: A remote, mostly shady cliff zone at the far end of the Jungle on the Aquarius Plateau in south-central Utah, up around 10,400 feet. The cliff band splits into a lower-angle wall of shorter pitches, about 40 to 60 feet, and a taller wall of better stone with room for longer lines. Nearly all of the twenty or so routes are alpine-style trad and sport on volcanic rock, spanning roughly 5.6 to 5.12 with the heart of the grades at 5.9 to 5.10. Trails with fixed aids lead in from above, and a steep chute offers a shortcut. Expect thin air, afternoon storms in midsummer and a quiet, committed atmosphere.
